facts.fact_text: On 14 July 2008 a demonstration was held in Diyarbakır.
The demonstration of 14 July 2008 in Diyarbakır was held to protest about the conditions of detention of Abdullah Öcalan.
According to the police report of 21 July 2008, people started to assemble by 4.30 p.m. on 14 July 2008 in front of the DTP party office in Diyarbakır.
According to the police report of 21 July 2008, by 5.50 p.m. on 14 July 2008 approximately 3,000 people had gathered in front of the DTP party office in Diyarbakır.
According to the police report of 21 July 2008, demonstrators started to march and arrived at Koşuyolu Park at 6.30 p.m. on 14 July 2008, where the press statement was made.
In his statement of 22 July 2008, the applicant stated that he joined the demonstrators and chanted the slogan "Long live President Öcalan" ("Biji Serok Apo") on 14 July 2008.

During the hearing of 21 October 2008, the applicant maintained that he had participated in the demonstration, chanted the slogan "Long live President Öcalan" ("Biji Serok Apo") and thrown stones at the police when they intervened.

The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court established in its judgment of 11 November 2008 that the applicant (Ferit Gülcü) actively took part in the illegal demonstrations held on 14 July 2008 in Diyarbakır in accordance with the instructions of the terrorist organisation PKK.

According to the police report of 21 July 2008, at 7 p.m. on 14 July 2008, while Emine Ayna, a Member of Parliament from the DTP, was giving a speech, a group of people started throwing stones at the police officers and the cars parked in the neighbourhood.

According to the police report of 21 July 2008, subsequent to the press statements on 14 July 2008, when the crowd dispersed, some people within the crowd knocked over waste containers and attacked the police and the shops in the neighbourhood with stones and bats while chanting slogans in support of the PKK and its leader.
According to the police report of 21 July 2008, the police intervened against the group on 14 July 2008 using truncheons, water and tear gas.

At the end of the police report of 21 July 2008, it was noted that, according to the video footage, the applicant had thrown stones at the police together with a number of other persons on 14 July 2008.
In four of the photographs from the police report of 21 July 2008, the applicant is seen in a group of young men while, according to the police, throwing stones at the security forces.
In his statement of 22 July 2008, the applicant stated that he threw stones at the police officers on 14 July 2008.
The applicant was arrested on 21 July 2008.
On 22 July 2008 the applicant was brought before a judge of the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court.

The judge of the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court remanded the applicant in custody on 22 July 2008 in view of the existence of a strong suspicion that he had committed the offence of "committing an offence on behalf of an illegal organisation without being a member of the organisation", in breach of Law no. 2911 (Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act).

The judge of the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court remanded the applicant in custody on 22 July 2008 in view of the existence of a strong suspicion that he had committed the offence of "dissemination of propaganda in support of a terrorist organisation", and having regard to the evidence.

The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court convicted the applicant under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), on the basis of Articles 220 § 6 and 314 § 3 of the same Code; section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713); and sections 23(b) and 33(c) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911).
The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court sentenced the applicant to a total of seven years and six months of imprisonment.

The judge of the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court remanded the applicant in custody on 22 July 2008 in view of the existence of a strong suspicion that he had committed the offence of "committing an offence on behalf of an illegal organisation without being a member of the organisation", in breach of Law no. 2911 (Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act).

The applicant was charged with membership of an illegal organisation as he was considered to have committed a crime on behalf of an illegal organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) on the basis of Articles 220 § 6 and 314 § 3 of the same Code.
The applicant was charged with resisting the security forces by way of throwing stones under sections 23(b) and 33(c) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911).
The applicant was charged with disseminating propaganda in support of the PKK under section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713).
The applicant was charged with denigration of the symbols of the sovereignty of the State under Article 300 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237).

At the material time, Article 220 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who establishes or directs organisations for the purpose of criminal activity shall be liable to imprisonment of between two and six years, provided that the structure of the organisation, the number of members, and the quantity of equipment and supplies are sufficient to commit the intended crimes.

At the material time, Article 220 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who becomes a member of an organisation established for the purpose of criminal activity shall be liable to imprisonment of between one and three years.

At the material time, Article 220 § 3 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that if the organisation is armed, the sentences stated in paragraphs 1 and 2 shall be increased by a proportion of between one quarter and one half.
At the material time, Article 220 § 4 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that any crime committed within the framework of the organisation's activities shall be punished separately.

At the material time, Article 220 § 5 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that the heads of the organisations shall also be sentenced as the perpetrators of all crimes committed within the framework of the organisation's activities.

At the material time, Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who commits a crime on behalf of the illegal organisation, even if they are not a member of that organisation, shall also be punished for being a member of the organisation.

At the material time, Article 220 § 7 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who aids and abets an illegal organisation knowingly and intentionally, even if they do not belong to the hierarchical structure of the organisation, shall be punished as a member of the organisation.

At the material time, Article 220 § 8 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who makes propaganda for the organisation or its objectives shall be punished by imprisonment of between one and three years, and if the said crime is committed through the media and press the sentence shall be increased by one half.

Article 314 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who forms an armed organisation to commit the crimes listed in the fourth and fifth sections of that chapter, or commands such an organisation, shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between ten and fifteen years.

Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who becomes a member of an armed organisation mentioned in Article 314 § 1 shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between five and ten years.

Article 314 § 3 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that other provisions relating to the crime of forming an organisation for the purpose of criminal activity are also applicable for the crime of membership of an armed organisation.

Article 300 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who publicly tears, burns or otherwise denigrates the Turkish flag shall be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of between one and three years, and that this provision applies to all signs bearing the white crescent and star on a red ground described in the Constitution as a symbol of the sovereignty of the State of the Republic of Turkey.

Article 265 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who uses methods of violence or threats against a public officer with a view to obstructing him or her in the execution of his or her duties shall be liable to imprisonment of between six months and three years.

According to section 23(b) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), in force at the material time, meetings or demonstration marches during which the demonstrators or the participants bear, inter alia, firearms, explosives, cutting and perforating tools, stones, bats, iron or rubber bars, wires, chains, poisons, gas or fog materials, were considered to be "unlawful meetings and demonstration marches".

Section 33(c) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), before it was amended by Law no. 6008 on 25 July 2010, provided that persons who show resistance with weapons or materials listed in section 23(b) while being dispersed during meetings and demonstration marches shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between five and eight years.

Following the amendments introduced by Law no. 6008, section 33 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) provided that persons who take part in meetings and demonstration marches while carrying weapons or materials listed in section 23(b) shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between six months and three years.

Following the amendments introduced by Law no. 6008, section 32(1) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) provides that persons taking part in unlawful meetings or demonstration marches who continue not to disperse despite warnings or use of force shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between six months and three years, and that if the offender is one of the organisers the sentence shall be increased by half.

Following the amendments introduced by Law no. 6008, section 32(2) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) provides that persons who resist the security forces by methods of violence or threats despite warnings or use of force shall also be punished for committing the crime proscribed by Article 265 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237).

By Law no. 6008 a new provision, section 34/A, was added to the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), providing that section 2(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) shall not be applicable to children who commit the crime of resistance during unlawful meetings and demonstration marches or who commit the crime of propaganda during meetings and demonstration marches in which they take part.

At the material time, section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) provided that any person who disseminates propaganda in support of a terrorist organisation shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between one and five years.

Section 2(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713), referred to in section 34/A of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), provides that persons who commit crimes on behalf of a terrorist organisation shall be considered as terror offenders even if they are not a member of that terrorist organisation.
Abdullah Öcalan is the leader of the PKK (Kurdish Workers' Party).
The PKK (Kurdish Workers' Party) is an illegal armed organisation.
The police took the necessary measures on 14 July 2008 as they suspected that there could be violent protests during the march, which could become a demonstration for the PKK.

According to the police report of 21 July 2008, at 7 p.m. on 14 July 2008, while Emine Ayna, a Member of Parliament from the DTP, was giving a speech, a group of people started throwing stones at the police officers and the cars parked in the neighbourhood.

According to the police report of 21 July 2008, subsequent to the press statements on 14 July 2008, when the crowd dispersed, some people within the crowd knocked over waste containers and attacked the police and the shops in the neighbourhood with stones and bats while chanting slogans in support of the PKK and its leader.
According to the police report of 21 July 2008, some people had taken down the Turkish flag in the schoolyard of the Diyarbakır nursery school on 14 July 2008.

At the end of the police report of 21 July 2008, it was noted that, according to the video footage, the applicant had thrown stones at the police together with a number of other persons on 14 July 2008.

At the end of the police report of 21 July 2008, it was noted that, according to the video footage, the applicant had acted with the group which had taken down the Turkish flag at the Diyarbakır nursery school on 14 July 2008.
The applicant was born in 1992.
The applicant was transferred to the children's branch of the Security Directorate after being found to be a minor subsequent to a medical check following his arrest on 21 July 2008.

The applicant's lawyer asked the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court on 22 July 2008 not to remand the applicant in custody, submitting that the applicant was a minor and therefore not capable of realising the meaning and consequences of his acts.
The public prosecutor requested that the sentences be reduced taking into account the fact that the applicant had been aged between 15 and 18 years old at the material time.

For the membership of an illegal organisation conviction, the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court reduced the sentence by one third by virtue of Article 31 § 3 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account that the applicant had been aged between 15 and 18 at the material time, resulting in five years.

For the membership of an illegal organisation conviction, the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court further reduced the sentence by one sixth under Article 62 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) taking into account the applicant's "sincere confessions" as well as his attitude and behaviour during the proceedings, resulting in a total of four years and two months of imprisonment.

For the propaganda conviction, the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court applied the minimum penalty of one year of imprisonment, then reduced it by one third by virtue of Article 31 § 3 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) taking into account the fact that the applicant had been aged between 15 and 18 at the material time, resulting in eight months.

For the propaganda conviction, the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court further reduced the sentence by one sixth under Article 62 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account the applicant's "sincere confessions" as well as his attitude and behaviour during the proceedings, resulting in a total of six months and twenty days.

For the resistance to security forces conviction, the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court applied the minimum penalty of five years' imprisonment, then reduced it by one third by virtue of Article 31 § 3 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account the fact that the applicant had been aged between 15 and 18 at the material time, resulting in three years and four months.

For the resistance to security forces conviction, the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court further reduced the sentence by one sixth under Article 62 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account the applicant's "sincere confessions" as well as his attitude and behaviour during the proceedings, resulting in a total of two years, nine months and ten days' imprisonment.

Diyarbakır Juvenile Court revoked the applicant's convictions contained in the judgment of 11 November 2008 of the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court, holding that the amendments applied by Law no. 6008 were in favour of the applicant.

Diyarbakır Juvenile Court acquitted the applicant of the charge of membership of a terrorist organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), having regard to section 34/A of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), which had entered into force on 25 July 2010 with Law no. 6008.
Diyarbakır Juvenile Court convicted the applicant of disseminating propaganda in support of a terrorist organisation under section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713).

For the propaganda conviction, Diyarbakır Juvenile Court applied the minimum penalty of one year of imprisonment, then reduced it by one third by virtue of Article 31 § 3 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account the fact that the applicant had been aged between 15 and 18 at the material time, resulting in eight months.

For the propaganda conviction, Diyarbakır Juvenile Court further reduced the sentence by one sixth under Article 62 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account the possible implications of the sentence for the minor, resulting in a total of six months and twenty days.

Diyarbakır Juvenile Court suspended the pronouncement of the propaganda judgment on condition that the applicant did not commit another wilful offence for a period of three years, in accordance with Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Law no. 5271) and Article 23 of the Code of Juvenile Protection (Law no. 5395), having regard to the length of the sentence and to the fact that the applicant did not have a criminal record.

Diyarbakır Juvenile Court convicted the applicant of participation in a demonstration while in possession of prohibited materials pursuant to section 33(1) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911).

For the conviction of participation in a demonstration while in possession of prohibited materials, Diyarbakır Juvenile Court applied the minimum penalty of six months' imprisonment, then reduced it by one third by virtue of Article 31 § 3 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account the fact that the applicant had been aged between 15 and 18 at the material time, resulting in four months.

For the conviction of participation in a demonstration while in possession of prohibited materials, Diyarbakır Juvenile Court further reduced the sentence by one sixth under Article 62 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account the possible implications of the sentence for the minor, resulting in a total of three months and ten days.

Diyarbakır Juvenile Court suspended the pronouncement of the judgment for participation in a demonstration while in possession of prohibited materials on condition that the applicant did not commit another wilful offence for a period of three years, in accordance with Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Law no. 5271) and Article 23 of the Code of Juvenile Protection (Law no. 5395), having regard to the length of the sentence and to the fact that the applicant did not have a criminal record.

Diyarbakır Juvenile Court convicted the applicant of resistance to the security forces which had used force to disperse the demonstrators pursuant to section 32(1) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911).

For the conviction of resistance to the security forces under section 32(1) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), Diyarbakır Juvenile Court applied the minimum penalty of six months' imprisonment, then reduced it by one third by virtue of Article 31 § 3 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account the fact that the applicant had been aged between 15 and 18 at the material time, resulting in four months.

For the conviction of resistance to the security forces under section 32(1) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), Diyarbakır Juvenile Court further reduced the sentence by one sixth under Article 62 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account the possible implications of the sentence for the minor, resulting in a total of three months and ten days.

Diyarbakır Juvenile Court suspended the pronouncement of the judgment for resistance to the security forces under section 32(1) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) on condition that the applicant did not commit another wilful offence for a period of three years, in accordance with Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Law no. 5271) and Article 23 of the Code of Juvenile Protection (Law no. 5395), having regard to the length of the sentence and to the fact that the applicant did not have a criminal record.

Diyarbakır Juvenile Court convicted the applicant of obstructing the security forces in the execution of their duties by way of resistance together with other persons and using the influence of an organisation pursuant to section 32(2) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) and Article 265 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237).

For the conviction under section 32(2) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) and Article 265 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), Diyarbakır Juvenile Court applied the minimum penalty of six months' imprisonment, then increased it by one third as the crime had been committed collectively, resulting in eight months.

For the conviction under section 32(2) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) and Article 265 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), Diyarbakır Juvenile Court further increased the sentence by one half pursuant to Article 265 § 4 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) as the crime had been committed using the influence of an organisation, resulting in twelve months.

For the conviction under section 32(2) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) and Article 265 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), Diyarbakır Juvenile Court reduced the sentence by one third by virtue of Article 31 § 3 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account the fact that the applicant had been aged between 15 and 18 at the material time, resulting in eight months.

For the conviction under section 32(2) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) and Article 265 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), Diyarbakır Juvenile Court further reduced the sentence by one sixth under Article 62 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account the possible implications of the sentence for a minor, resulting in a total of six months and twenty days.

Diyarbakır Juvenile Court suspended the pronouncement of the judgment for the conviction under section 32(2) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) and Article 265 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) on condition that the applicant did not commit another wilful offence for a period of three years, in accordance with Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Law no. 5271) and Article 23 of the Code of Juvenile Protection (Law no. 5395), having regard to the length of the sentence and to the fact that the applicant did not have a criminal record.

On 21 February 2007 the Ninth Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of Diyarbakır Assize Court in the case of F.Ö., holding that F.Ö.'s acts constituted not only the offences proscribed in section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) and section 32(1) and (3) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), but also membership of an illegal organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) on the basis of Articles 220 § 6 and 314 § 3 of the same Code, as he had committed those offences on behalf of the organisation.

The Ninth Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation considered that F.Ö. should be punished for having committed the offence of membership of an illegal organisation and the other offences proscribed in section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) and section 32(1) and (3) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911).

Diyarbakır Assize Court stated in its judgment of 31 May 2007 in the case of F.Ö. that in cases where people participate in funerals of members of a terrorist organisation or in Newroz celebrations subsequent to abstract and generalised calls of that organisation, and where chanting slogans constitutes propaganda for that organisation, it is not possible to state that those crimes were committed on behalf of the organisation.

Diyarbakır Assize Court stated in its judgment of 31 May 2007 in the case of F.Ö. that in order for a court to conclude that a crime was committed on behalf of an organisation, the organisation must have called for action not to an undefined collective, but rather to an individual person who is capable of directly committing that act.

The Plenary Court of Cassation (Criminal Divisions) held in its decision of 4 March 2008 that the PKK's public call had been made concrete through broadcasts from media organs of the organisation and there is no need for such calls to target identified individual persons.

The Plenary Court of Cassation (Criminal Divisions) held in its decision of 4 March 2008 that the acts carried out on behalf of the PKK were within the knowledge of the organisation and in line with its will, and that the acts of an accused who participates in such acts constitute a breach of Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) on the basis of Articles 220 § 6 and 314 § 3 of the same Code.

The Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted by the General Assembly of the United Nations on 20 November 1989 and has binding force under international law vis-à-vis the Contracting States, including all member States of the Council of Europe.

Article 1 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child states that a child means every human being below the age of eighteen years unless under the law applicable to the child, majority is attained earlier.

Article 3 § 1 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child provides that in all actions concerning children, whether undertaken by public or private social welfare institutions, courts of law, administrative authorities or legislative bodies, the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration.

Article 37(b) of the Convention on the Rights of the Child provides that no child shall be deprived of his or her liberty unlawfully or arbitrarily, and that the arrest, detention or imprisonment of a child shall be in conformity with the law and shall be used only as a measure of last resort and for the shortest appropriate period of time.

Article 37(c) of the Convention on the Rights of the Child provides that every child deprived of liberty shall be treated with humanity and respect for the inherent dignity of the human person, and in a manner which takes into account the needs of persons of his or her age.

Article 40 § 1 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child provides that States Parties recognize the right of every child alleged as, accused of, or recognized as having infringed the penal law to be treated in a manner consistent with the promotion of the child's sense of dignity and worth, which reinforces the child's respect for the human rights and fundamental freedoms of others and which takes into account the child's age and the desirability of promoting the child's reintegration and the child's assuming a constructive role in society.

Article 40 § 3(b) of the Convention on the Rights of the Child provides that States Parties shall seek to promote measures for dealing with children in conflict with the law without resorting to judicial proceedings, providing that human rights and legal safeguards are fully respected.

Article 40 § 4 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child provides that a variety of dispositions, such as care, guidance and supervision orders, counselling, probation, foster care, education and vocational training programmes and other alternatives to institutional care shall be available to ensure that children are dealt with in a manner appropriate to their well-being and proportionate both to their circumstances and the offence.

General Comment No. 10 of the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child, dated 25 April 2007, states that children in conflict with the law have the right to be treated in ways that promote their reintegration and the child's assuming a constructive role in society, and that the arrest, detention or imprisonment of a child may be used only as a measure of last resort.

General Comment No. 10 of the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child, dated 25 April 2007, states that when judicial proceedings are initiated, the juvenile justice system should provide for ample opportunities to deal with children in conflict with the law by using social and/or educational measures, and to strictly limit the use of deprivation of liberty, and in particular pre-trial detention, as a measure of last resort.

General Comment No. 10 of the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child, dated 25 April 2007, states that the reaction to an offence should always be in proportion not only to the circumstances and the gravity of the offence, but also to the age, lesser culpability, circumstances and needs of the child, as well as to the various and particularly long-term needs of the society, and that a strictly punitive approach is not in accordance with the leading principles for juvenile justice.

In its Resolution 2010 (2014), adopted on 27 June 2014 and entitled "Child-friendly juvenile justice: from rhetoric to reality", the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe called on member States to establish a specialised juvenile justice system, set the minimum age of criminal responsibility at at least 14 years of age, prohibit exceptions to the minimum age of criminal responsibility, and ensure that detention of juveniles is used as a measure of last resort and for the shortest possible period of time.

In its Resolution 2010 (2014) of 27 June 2014, the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe called on member States to develop a broad range of alternative non-custodial measures and sanctions, abolish life imprisonment for children, establish a reasonable maximum period to which a child may be sentenced, and develop a broad range of diversion programmes based on principles of restorative justice.

The Recommendation of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe on social reactions to juvenile delinquency (R (87)20), adopted on 17 September 1987 at the 410th meeting of the Ministers' Deputies, recommended that governments of member states review their legislation and practice with a view to excluding the remand in custody of minors, apart from exceptional cases of very serious offences committed by older minors, and in such cases restricting the length of remand in custody and keeping minors apart from adults.

The Recommendation on the European Rules for juvenile offenders subject to sanctions or measures (CM/Rec(2008)11), adopted by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe on 5 November 2008, provides that the imposition and implementation of sanctions or measures shall be based on the best interests of the juvenile offenders, limited by the gravity of the offences committed, and take account of their age, physical and mental well-being, development, capacities and personal circumstances.

The Recommendation CM/Rec(2008)11, adopted by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe on 5 November 2008, provides that deprivation of liberty of a juvenile shall be a measure of last resort and imposed and implemented for the shortest period possible, and that special efforts must be undertaken to avoid pre-trial detention.

In his report published on 1 October 2009 (CommDH(2009)30), following his visit to Turkey on 28 June to 3 July 2009, Mr Thomas Hammarberg, the former Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe, stated that over the previous nine months approximately 250 children of Kurdish origin, more than 190 of them between 13 and 17 years of age, had been arrested and detained after having taken part in demonstrations organised by Kurdish groups and thrown stones at police forces.

In his report published on 1 October 2009 (CommDH(2009)30), Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that four children aged between 16 and 17 had been detained in the Diyarbakır prison since 14 July 2008, charged with membership of a terrorist organization as a result of participating in a protest in Diyarbakır.

In his report published on 1 October 2009 (CommDH(2009)30), Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that prosecution in such cases is often based on Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), and that the extensive use of this provision by courts against participants of Kurdish-related demonstrations follows a ruling of the General Criminal Board of the Court of Cassation in March 2008.

In his report published on 1 October 2009 (CommDH(2009)30), Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that it appears necessary to revisit certain over-restrictive provisions of the legislation, including Criminal Code Articles 301 and 220, which have been used in a manner that has unjustifiably suppressed freedom of expression.

In his report published on 12 July 2011 (CommDH(2011)25), following his visit to Turkey on 27 to 29 April 2011, Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that his deep concern about the application of Article 220 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), and in particular its paragraphs 6 and 8, expressed following his 2009 visit, remains valid in the context of freedom of expression and freedom of the media in Turkey.

In his report published on 10 January 2012 (CommDH(2012)2), following his visit to Turkey on 10 to 14 October 2011, Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that he was particularly preoccupied by the wide interpretation of the courts concerning the definition of offences and their constitutive acts under the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) and Article 220 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237).

In his report published on 10 January 2012 (CommDH(2012)2), Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that persons participating in demonstrations following public calls by the PKK were brought into the ambit of Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), in accordance with a ruling of the Court of Cassation in March 2008.

In his report published on 10 January 2012 (CommDH(2012)2), Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that the application of Article 220 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), as well as of Articles 6 and 7 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713), continues to raise serious concerns.

In his report published on 10 January 2012 (CommDH(2012)2), Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that violence or the threat to use violence is an essential component of an act of terrorism, and that restrictions of human rights in the fight against terrorism must be defined as precisely as possible and be necessary and proportionate to the aim pursued.

In his report published on 10 January 2012 (CommDH(2012)2), Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that the provisions contained in the Turkish anti-terror legislation and Article 220 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) allow for a very wide margin of appreciation, in particular in cases where membership in a terrorist organisation has not been proven and when an act or statement may be deemed to coincide with the aims or instructions of a terrorist organisation.

In his comments of 20 February 2012, Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that while the proposed amendments to Article 220 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) could have short-term benefits, they do not offer a lasting solution to serious problems caused by Article 220, and that the main concern is the fact that Article 220 allows for a very wide margin of appreciation in cases where membership in a terrorist organisation has not been proven.

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that many hundreds of people in Turkey face prosecution or are serving substantial sentences for terrorism convictions for engaging in peaceful protest or throwing stones or burning a tire at a protest, and that legal amendments since 2005 and case law since 2008 have allowed courts to convict demonstrators under the harshest terrorism laws.

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that criminal justice officials have deemed Kurdish protestors to be 'committing crimes on behalf of the PKK without being a member of that organization' under Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), resulting in prosecution as if they were armed 'members' of the PKK under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237).

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that the majority of adults convicted under these laws have received prison terms of between seven and 15 years, and that prior to a July 2010 legal amendment, child protestors typically received prison sentences of between four and five years.

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that in none of the cases examined by Human Rights Watch had prosecutors submitted evidence to establish that the individual defendant either heard the PKK's 'appeal' or had been directly instructed or motivated by the PKK to participate in the demonstration, or had any other specific link with the PKK.

The Amnesty International report of 17 June 2010 stated that children alleged to have participated in demonstrations are frequently prosecuted under section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) and under Article 314 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) via Article 220 § 6 of the same Code, following a ruling of the Supreme Court of Appeals (case number 2007/9282).

The Amnesty International report of 17 June 2010 stated that children who have been prosecuted in connection with their participation in demonstrations have frequently faced multiple charges for the same act, including making propaganda for a terrorist organisation, membership of a terrorist organisation and violation of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911).

The Amnesty International report of 17 June 2010 stated that by law, children aged 15-17 are tried in Special Heavy Penal courts under the same procedures as adults for terrorism-related offences, pursuant to Article 9 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713), with hearings closed to the public.

The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) allows the state to punish individuals who have not been proven in court to be members of a terrorist organisation as though they were, if deemed to have performed a criminal act 'in the name of an organization'.

The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that courts have used Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) as the basis for imposing increased sentences with little evidence of the commission of a recognizably criminal offence or any demonstrable link to a 'terrorist organization', and that the evidence frequently amounts to nothing more than participation in demonstrations or the writing of pro-Kurdish articles.
